passages.title: Weather vs. Climate
paragraphs: "Weather" and "climate" sound almost the same. But they answer two different questions. Weather is what's happening outside right now, or this week. Is it raining? Is it sunny? Is it cold or warm? Weather can change very fast. It can be sunny in the morning. It can be rainy by afternoon. It can be different again tomorrow. That's why weather forecasters can only predict a few days ahead. It's a fast-changing system. It's hard to predict far into the future.

Climate is different. Climate is the usual pattern of weather in a place. We measure it over many, many years. A desert's climate is usually hot and dry. That doesn't mean it never rains there. It means rain is rare, on average, over time. A place near the ocean usually has a mild climate. It is not too hot, and not too cold. This is true even though its daily weather still changes from day to day.
So if someone asks, "what's the weather like?" they want to know about today. If they ask, "what's the climate like?" they want to know about the usual pattern, over many years, not just today.

passages.title: Weather vs. Climate
paragraphs: News reports sometimes mix up two words. The words are weather and climate. They do not mean the same thing.

Weather means what is happening in one place right now. It means the temperature, the rain, and the wind, on a given day. Weather is hard to predict far ahead. Small changes today can lead to very different results a week later. Even the best forecasts get shaky after about ten days.

Climate is different. Climate is the usual pattern of weather in a region. It is measured over many years, not one day. A region's climate does not tell you tomorrow's weather. It tells you the chances of different kinds of weather over a long time.

This difference matters in real life. Say it snows during a week that is usually warm. That is just one weather event. It does not prove the climate is changing. One cold day does not undo the fact that summer, on average, is hotter than winter.

Knowing this difference is a useful skill. It lets you read a headline about one storm without panicking. A single event tells you about today. It does not tell you much about the bigger, longer pattern.
